kaps_punt: Medisyne en dokters: siektes, anatomie, fisiologie en kliniese eksamens

items.bewering: Die dokters van ou Egipte het verbande van linne om wonde gedraai.
items.blok: Dokters vir wonde en gebreekte bene
items.bron: Mayall, 'Ancient Egyptian surgery', Medical Journal of Australia 2014 (mja.com.au/journal/2014/200/1/ancient-egyptian-surgery): wounds closed and dressed with 'adhesive strips of linen'; Bone & Joint 360 (boneandjoint.org.uk, 10.1302/2048-0105.22.360124): Naga ed-Deir splints 'held in place with linen bandages'; 1928 press report of Breasted's translation (paperspast.natlib.govt.nz MT19280608.2.21) lists linen bandages made for surgical use.

items.bewering: As 'n wond wyd oop was, het hulle dit met steke toegemaak.
items.blok: Dokters vir wonde en gebreekte bene
items.bron: Wikipedia, Edwin Smith Papyrus: wounds closed 'with sutures (for wounds of the lip, throat, and shoulder)'; MJA 2014 quotes case 10, a gaping wound over the eyebrow: 'after thou hast stitched it . . . bind fresh meat upon it'. MJA also notes that archaeologically the only sutures actually found are in embalming wounds, so the evidence for surgical stitching is textual; the lesson's sentence is grounded in the papyrus, which the next block names as the source.

items.bewering: Hierdie geneeshere het gebreekte bene gespalk
items.blok: Dokters vir wonde en gebreekte bene
items.bron: MJA 2014: humerus fracture, 'thou shouldst make for him two splints of linen'; Bone & Joint 360: two Fifth Dynasty graves at Naga ed-Deir with linen-wrapped palm-bark splints still in place; Wikipedia, Edwin Smith Papyrus lists splints among treatments.

items.bewering: en medisyne van plante gemaak.
items.blok: Dokters vir wonde en gebreekte bene
items.bron: World Archaeology, 'Egyptian medicine' (world-archaeology.com/features/egyptian-medicine): Ebers papyrus ingredients include opium, henna, garlic, coriander and juniper; MJA 2014: pain remedies of myrtle, dill, lettuce, cumin and linseed, and mandrake; Wikipedia, Ancient Egyptian medicine: medicinal use of plants 'is known to be extensive'.

items.bewering: Ons weet dit uit ou geskrifte op papirus.
items.bron: Linen, stitching and splints are described in the Edwin Smith papyrus and plant remedies in the Ebers papyrus (Wikipedia, Edwin Smith Papyrus; Wikipedia, Ebers Papyrus; MJA 2014). The sentence does not claim papyri are the only evidence; splinted bones from Naga ed-Deir graves also exist (Bone & Joint 360), which does not make it false.

items.bewering: Twee daarvan dra die name van die mans wat dit meer as 150 jaar gelede gekoop het.
items.bron: Edwin Smith bought the surgical papyrus at Luxor in 1862 (Wikipedia, Edwin Smith Papyrus; SUNY Buffalo history-of-communication-disorders page, acsu.buffalo.edu/~duchan: 20 January 1862, from Mustapha Agha), 164 years ago. Georg Ebers bought the Ebers papyrus at Luxor on his 1872/73 journey (Wikipedia, Georg Ebers; Leipzig University Library says acquired 1873; Wikipedia, Ebers Papyrus also gives winter 1873-74). Every date given is between 152 and 154 years before 2026, so 'meer as 150 jaar' holds on all of them.

items.bewering: Die Ebers-papirus is sowat 3 500 jaar oud.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Ebers Papyrus: written c. 1550 BCE (about 3 575 years ago); Leipzig University Library (via search summary): origin at the end of the 16th century BCE, confirmed by the calendar on the verso and radiocarbon dating in 2014. 'Sowat 3 500' is a fair rounding.

items.bewering: Dit beskryf baie siektes met hulle simptome en gee honderde middels daarteen.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Ebers Papyrus: covers intestinal disease, eye and skin problems, gynaecology, abscesses and tumours, burns, mental disorders, and contains 'over 842' formulas and remedies; other summaries give about 700. Symptom descriptions occur (e.g. rubric 197, whose symptoms are debated as possible diabetes). 'Honderde' is correct on either count.

items.bewering: Die Edwin Smith-papirus beskryf 48 gevalle
items.bron: Wikipedia, Edwin Smith Papyrus: 'describes 48 cases of injuries, fractures, wounds, dislocations and tumors'; SUNY Buffalo page (acsu.buffalo.edu/~duchan): 48 cases, head (1-27) down to spine (48).

items.bewering: en die meeste daarvan is beserings.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Edwin Smith Papyrus: 'The vast majority of the papyrus is concerned with trauma and surgery'; the few non-injury cases are tumours/abscesses in the chest section. 'Die meeste' is correctly narrower than 'almal'.

items.bewering: By elkeen ondersoek die dokter eers die pasiënt: hy kyk, vra vrae en voel met sy vingers.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Edwin Smith Papyrus: 'Each case details the type of the injury, examination of the patient, diagnosis and prognosis, and treatment'; examination used 'visual and olfactory clues, palpation and taking of the pulse'. Questioning is attested: case 20, 'if thou ask of him concerning his malady and he speak not to thee', and case 22 (SUNY Buffalo page, acsu.buffalo.edu/~duchan). Feeling with the fingers: case 20 'if thou puttest thy fingers on the mouth of that wound', case 44 ribs that 'crepitate under his fingers' (MJA 2014). Note for a person: every case opens with an examination, but questioning is attested in only some cases, not all 48. I read the colon as describing what the examination consisted of across the papyrus, which is true; it would be inaccurate only if read as a checklist all three methods follow in every single case.

items.bewering: Dan maak hy 'n diagnose en sê wat fout is. Laastens besluit hy of hy iets daaraan kan doen.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Edwin Smith Papyrus and SUNY Buffalo page: after the examination comes the diagnosis and then one of three verdicts, 'An ailment which I will treat', 'An ailment with which I will contend', 'An ailment not to be treated' (14 of the 48 cases). The order examination - diagnosis - verdict is correct; treatment instructions follow the verdict where one is given, so 'laastens' is right as the last step of the doctor's judgement.

items.bewering: Anatomie is kennis van die dele van die liggaam en waar elkeen lê.
items.bron: Britannica: anatomy is concerned with 'the identification and description of the body structures of living things'; Britannica Kids: anatomy concerns the structure of living things. Same wording in the begrip entry.

items.bewering: Die dokters het geweet die hart is 'n baie belangrike deel.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Ebers Papyrus: contains a 'treatise on the heart' treating it as the centre of the blood supply with vessels to every part of the body; Museo Egizio catalogue Cat. 1192 (collezioni.museoegizio.it): the heart regarded as the seat of intelligence and memory.

items.bewering: Hulle het ook geweet dat skade aan die kop ander dele van die liggaam kan raak.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Edwin Smith Papyrus: 'The influence of brain injuries on parts of the body is recognized, such as paralysis'; SUNY Buffalo page: head cases 20 and 22 record speechlessness and neck stiffness after temple injuries.

items.bewering: Fisiologie is kennis van hoe die dele van die liggaam werk.
items.bron: Britannica: physiology is the 'study of the functioning of living organisms ... and of the functioning of their constituent tissues or cells'; Britannica Kids: how structures work. Same wording in the begrip entry.

items.bewering: Die dokters het geglo kanale loop van die hart af deur die hele liggaam.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Ebers Papyrus: the heart as centre of the blood supply 'with vessels attached for every part of the body'; the channels are called metu (Médecine/Sciences 2004 abstract, 'Concepts of the heart in Ancient Egypt', PubMed 15067585, via search summary: communication of the heart guaranteed by a network of vessels named metu).

items.bewering: Hulle het geglo die kanale dra bloed, ander soorte vloeistof en lug.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Ancient Egyptian medicine: 'channels' that 'carried air, water, and blood to the body'; Wikipedia, Ebers Papyrus: vessels carrying blood, tears, urine and semen.

items.bewering: Hulle het gedink jy word siek as 'n kanaal verstop raak.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Ancient Egyptian medicine: by analogy with Nile irrigation, a blocked channel made things unhealthy, and physicians used laxatives to unblock the 'channels'; Wikipedia, Ebers Papyrus: the 'channel theory' held that unimpeded flow was necessary for health.

items.bewering: Hulle het ook die hartklop met hulle vingers gevoel.
items.bron: Wikipedia, Ancient Egyptian medicine: 'Egyptian physicians were aware of the existence of the pulse and its connection to the heart'; Wikipedia, Edwin Smith Papyrus: examination included 'taking of the pulse'; the case 1 gloss has the physician lay his fingers on the head, hands, pulse and feet and so 'measure the heart' (quoted in several translations; the passage has lacunae).

items.bewering: Die Egiptenare het verkeerd geglo dat 'n mens met die hart dink, nie met die brein nie.
items.bron: Museo Egizio catalogue Cat. 1192 (collezioni.museoegizio.it/en-GB/material/Cat_1192): the Egyptians regarded the heart 'as the seat of intelligence and memory'; Médecine/Sciences 2004 (PubMed 15067585, via search summary): the heart was 'the seat of intelligence'. That thinking happens in the brain is modern consensus, so 'verkeerd' is right.

items.bewering: Dokters het dikwels ook 'n gebed of 'n towerspreuk oor die siek mens opgesê.
items.bron: World Archaeology, 'Egyptian medicine': 'Spells were recited, after which there was a laying on of hands', and even the Edwin Smith papyrus has incantations against disease-causing agents; Wikipedia, Ebers Papyrus: 'many incantations' to drive off disease-causing demons; MJA 2014: healers did not separate rational treatment from religion and magic. 'Dikwels' fits; the Edwin Smith trauma cases are the least magical (one case), which the sentence does not deny.

items.bewering: Vir hulle was dit sinvol, want hulle het geglo die gode kan genees.
items.bron: World Archaeology, 'Egyptian medicine': a patient's inscription that the god 'healed him on that very day'; Wikipedia, Ancient Egyptian medicine: Imhotep raised to a deity 'of medicine and healing'; Sekhmet and Thoth invoked for medical problems (historyskills / worldhistory summaries).

items.bewering: papirus: Velle om op te skryf, wat die Egiptenare van 'n plant langs die Nyl gemaak het.
items.bron: Britannica, 'papyrus (writing material)': made from the pith of Cyperus papyrus, long cultivated in the Nile delta, cut into strips, pressed and dried into sheets; the chief writing material of ancient Egypt.

items.bewering: simptoom: Iets wat 'n siek mens voel, soos pyn of 'n seer keel.
items.bron: EBSCO Research Starters, 'Understanding disease signs and symptoms', and EUPATI glossary: a symptom is subjective, experienced and reported by the person (e.g. headache, fatigue), as against a sign observed by someone else. Pain and a sore throat are standard symptoms.

items.bewering: diagnose: Die antwoord wat 'n dokter ná 'n ondersoek gee oor watter siekte of besering iemand het.
items.bron: EBSCO Research Starters and GoodRx 'signs vs symptoms': a provider uses symptoms, signs and tests to make a diagnosis, i.e. to identify the disease or condition (Merriam-Webster's page refused the fetch). Including 'besering' fits the Edwin Smith cases, which diagnose injuries.

items.bewering: anatomie: Kennis van die dele van die liggaam en waar elkeen lê.
items.bron: Britannica (see the study-block item above); identical to the study text, so the two cannot disagree.

items.bewering: fisiologie: Kennis van hoe die dele van die liggaam werk.
items.bron: Britannica (see the study-block item above); identical to the study text.

items.bewering: spalk: Om 'n gebreekte been stewig vas te bind teen hout of iets anders wat styf is, sodat dit nie beweeg nie.
items.bron: Merriam-Webster: a splint is material or a device used 'to protect and immobilize a body part'; Webster's 1913: 'a thin piece of wood, or other substance, used to keep in place ... a broken bone'. The Egyptian splints (palm bark or linen-stiffened boards bound with linen, Bone & Joint 360) fit the definition.

opsomming: All 29 checkable claims are confirmed and there are no analogies in the lesson. The only superlative is 'die meeste' for the Edwin Smith cases, and it is correctly narrower than 'all'. One wording a person may want to look at: 'By elkeen ondersoek die dokter eers die pasiënt: hy kyk, vra vrae en voel met sy vingers'. Every case does begin with an examination, but the papyrus records the doctor asking questions in only some cases, so the sentence is true as a description of how the examination was done and not as a list all three methods follow in every case.
